title: The Quantum Theory Where Particles Have Positions
hook: Pilot-wave theory takes the radical step of saying particles always have definite positions, guided by the wave function. It reproduces all of quantum mechanics — at a price.
key_points: De Broglie–Bohm theory is the most influential hidden-variable reading of quantum mechanics.
Particles have definite trajectories at all times; the wave function acts as a guiding field.
It reproduces standard quantum predictions, including the Born rule for probabilities, which it derives rather than postulates.
The price is explicit nonlocality and awkward extensions to spin and relativistic settings.
This review examines the theory's main formulations and argues about whether it is really simpler than textbook quantum mechanics.
content_html: Standard quantum mechanics says a particle has no definite position until you measure it. Pilot-wave theory, worked out by Louis de Broglie and later David Bohm, refuses that: particles always have positions and follow trajectories, and the wave function is a real field that guides them. Run the double-slit experiment and each electron really does go through one slit — the guiding wave, passing through both, is what steers it into the interference pattern.
extra_html: Andrea Oldofredi's review walks through the theory's main formulations and the questions they raise: where the Born rule for probabilities comes from (here something to be derived, not assumed), what the wave function actually is, how spin fits into a picture built on positions, and how far the approach can be pushed beyond non-relativistic quantum mechanics. Oldofredi also weighs the frequent claim that pilot-wave theory is conceptually simpler than the textbook version — it eliminates measurement collapse, but it buys that with an unavoidable, explicit nonlocality. The theory matters less as a likely replacement than as a proof of concept: quantum predictions do not force you to give up definite reality, they only make it expensive.

related.title: What Makes Quantum Physics Weird
related.hook: In the quantum world energy comes in lumps, particles act like waves, and you can't pin down everything at once — and yet it's our best-tested theory.

related.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
related.hook: Nature sets a hard limit: the more precisely you know where a particle is, the less you can know about how it's moving. It's not sloppy measurement — it's built into reality.

related.title: Can Classical Probability Alone Explain the Double-Slit Pattern?
related.hook: The double-slit interference pattern is physics' go-to symbol of quantum weirdness. A theoretical study shows classical probability alone can reproduce it, given the right ingredients.

related.title: Is Light a Wave or a Particle?
related.hook: Light behaves like a wave in some experiments and like a stream of particles in others — and the surprising answer is that it's both.

related.title: Quantum Entanglement
related.hook: Two particles can share one quantum state so tightly that measuring one instantly fixes the other's matching property — even light-years apart. Einstein called it spooky.

flashcards.prompt: What is the central claim of de Broglie–Bohm pilot-wave theory?
flashcards.back_html: Particles have definite positions and trajectories at all times; the wave function is a real guiding field that steers them. Nothing "collapses."

flashcards.prompt: How does pilot-wave theory treat the Born rule for quantum probabilities?

choices.text: It derives the rule rather than postulating it
It rejects the rule and predicts different probabilities
It postulates the rule exactly as standard quantum mechanics does

flashcards.explanation_html: Because the particle trajectories are definite, the statistics of measurement outcomes become something to explain — and the origin of the Born rule is one of the theory's main topics.

flashcards.prompt: What does pilot-wave theory pay for restoring definite trajectories?
flashcards.back_html: Explicit nonlocality, plus awkwardness in handling spin and in extending beyond non-relativistic quantum mechanics.
